reading.body:
Banking is where AI governance predates the AI boom by more than a decade: Fed SR 11-7 model risk rules already cover credit and AML models, and generative AI in service and compliance is the new supervised frontier.

The pattern is that banking's AI oversight is older than the current generative wave. Credit and AML models have operated under SR 11-7 since 2011, so the sector enters the generative era with pre-existing validation, documentation, and model risk requirements. Treasury's report frames the supervisory conversation, and the Evident AI Banking Index provides a public scoreboard across talent, innovation, leadership, and transparency.

For AI specifically, this means generative deployments in service and compliance inherit a governance burden that most other industries lack. A bank cannot launch a customer-facing chatbot or compliance assistant without treating it as a model under SR 11-7, which slows deployment but also reduces the chance of unmanaged failures. The data does not show scale. It contains no figures on compute demand or power consumption for banking AI, and no adoption rates or model sizes. Governance is the constraint the data documents, not infrastructure.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey puts AI use in finance and insurance, NAICS 52, at 41.0% in the latest reading, up from 36.5% in the prior period. The question asked is whether the business used AI in the last two weeks, and the first time it was asked was September 2023. That makes banking and insurance one of the more measured adopters in the survey rather than a sector that only talks about the technology.

What banks actually do with AI is not new in its foundations. Fraud detection and credit models have been in place for decades, and generative AI in service and compliance is described as the new frontier. The Evident AI Index, which benchmarks and tracks AI adoption across financial services, scores the major global banks across dozens of quantitative maturity metrics including talent, innovation, leadership and transparency, and is described as the closest thing banking has to a public AI scoreboard. Evident also notes that while tech companies have drawn the spotlight in the initial wave of AI hype, several of the world's biggest banks have quietly become AI-powered behemoths, and that banks are racing to incorporate the technology into almost everything they do.

On the vendor and model side, this site's Financial Models section tracks the 1000 most-downloaded open financial models on the Hugging Face Hub, with licence, downloads and release date, refreshed daily, covering models tuned for financial text. That is a catalogue of what is publicly available rather than a count of what banks have bought, and the sources here do not report spending figures or vendor market shares for the sector.

The governance picture is unusual because it predates the current boom. Credit and AML models operate under the Federal Reserve's SR 11-7 model risk management guidance, issued in 2011, and the letter is listed in the Fed's 2011 supervisory letters index. The sourced points describe banking as the sector where AI governance predates the AI boom by more than a decade. Separately, Treasury's report on AI in financial services, covering uses, opportunities and risks, is described as framing the US supervisory conversation. The excerpt from the Treasury page in this data concerns OFAC sanctions on a gold smuggling and money laundering network, not AI supervision, so it supports only that Treasury is active on financial crime enforcement, not the content of the AI report.

The sources here do not report ROI figures for banking AI, nor do they quantify deployment by use case beyond the general descriptions above. A reader deciding whether to deploy should take away that the compliance scaffolding already exists in the form of SR 11-7 model risk management, that peer adoption is measurable and rising according to the Census Bureau, and that public benchmarking through the Evident AI Index gives a way to compare maturity rather than guess at it.

https://evidentinsights.com/.brief: Evident Insights describes itself as an intelligence platform that benchmarks and tracks AI adoption across financial services, offering data, research and benchmarking to leaders in the sector. It publishes the Evident AI Index, which it says has generated debate and press coverage since launching in January 2023, and notes that its CEO, Alexandra Mousavizadeh, is a regular commentator on global AI trends. The page promotes a 2026 edition of the index for banks, due in October, along with insurance and Latin America editions and an annual invitation-only symposium for senior AI leaders in finance. It also cites a newsletter with over 15,000 subscribers and references coverage suggesting banks are racing to adopt AI while tech hiring in finance grows more competitive.

https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-rel.brief: On International Anti-Corruption Day, Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctioned 28 individuals and businesses tied to a Zimbabwe-based gold smuggling and money-laundering network led by Kamlesh Pattni. The Treasury says the scheme bribed officials, used trusted supporters to conceal ownership, and built a global web of companies to hide illicit activity, depriving Zimbabwe’s citizens of resource benefits while enriching corrupt officials and criminals. Acting Under Secretary Bradley T. Smith noted that “Corruption respects no borders” and that the action demonstrates a whole-of-government approach and collaboration with allies. The Treasury’s move is carried out under Executive Order 13818, which targets serious human-rights abuse and corruption worldwide. International Anti-Corruption Day, observed annually on December 9 since the 2003 UNCAC, aims to raise awareness of anti-corruption initiatives; the United Nations lists 189 parties to the convention.

https://www.federalreserve.gov/supervisi.brief: This page lists the Federal Reserve Board of Governors’ 2011 supervision and regulation letters. It notes that a lock icon or https indicates a secure .gov connection and advises “Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.” It also contains guidance on prior notices concerning dividend declarations by savings association subsidiaries of savings and loan holding companies.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/te.brief: The page catalogues the 1000 most-downloaded open financial models on the Hugging Face Hub, listing each model's licence, download count and release date, and is refreshed daily. The site states the data comes from the Hugging Face Hub public API, sorted by all-time downloads, with every model linking to its own Hub page. The page was last verified on 2026-10-05 and is offered free to read, cite and query. It also notes that SRJ Consulting & Services has published a novel about AI, "The AI Lawyer", due out 17 August 2026, and lists books by Stephen R. Jordan.
